notes.h: Social changes: who forms a family and when (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Social changes are shifts in how people live, marry and think. They have altered who forms a family, when families start and how big they are, which is why the Irish family is now more varied than it used to be.
points: Divorce has been possible since 1997 under the Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996. Separation and divorce increased the number of lone-parent families, and new partnerships formed afterwards created blended families, so there are more family types.

Cohabitation (an unmarried couple living together) is now a common alternative to marriage, and a growing proportion of children are born outside marriage. This means marriage is no longer the only basis of a family.
Later marriage and later first births, helped by family planning and by women's choices about education and work, have led to smaller families with fewer children per family.

Same-sex marriage (approved by referendum on 22 May 2015 under the Marriage Act 2015) and civil partnership (under the 2010 Act, in force from 1 January 2011) mean same-sex couples can form families. Adoption by same-sex couples makes same-sex parent families a recognised structure.
Surrogacy and assisted reproduction are also social issues. They give some couples new routes to parenthood.
Changing attitudes to lone parents mean lone-parent families are more widely accepted than in the past, so there is less pressure to marry in order to raise a family.
notes.tip: Link every change to a family structure or consequence, such as lone-parent, blended or smaller families. Do not say divorce caused family breakdown. Say it gave people more choice and changed the structures.

notes.h: Social changes: roles, beliefs, place and age (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Other social changes affect how family members share roles, where they live and how long generations stay connected. Each one changes who lives together and who looks after whom.
points: Gender equality in education and employment has produced more dual-career couples (both partners in a career), more shared household roles and, in some families, a father as the main carer.

Declining religious influence has weakened the Church's influence on decisions about marriage and family life. A more multi-denominational and multicultural society also gives people more choice in how they form families, so a wider range of family types exists.

Urbanisation, the movement from rural areas to towns and cities, loosened links with the extended family (grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins). Fewer relatives live nearby, so households are smaller and more often nuclear (parents and children only).
Children are dependent on their parents for longer because they spend more years in education, so adult children stay at home longer.
Increased life expectancy means more generations are alive at the same time and there are more older people, who need more care from their families.
Addiction, for example to alcohol or drugs, affects family life by causing stress, financial strain and conflict, and can change who takes on caring roles.
notes.tip: Where a change could fit two headings, choose one heading and say why. Religion, gender equality, urbanisation and cohabitation are social changes, not economic ones.

notes.h: Economic changes affecting family structure (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Economic pressures shape how many adults earn, where families live and whether relatives share a home. Money and jobs therefore decide family size, location and roles as well as living standards.
points: The cost of living, housing and childcare has risen, so both parents often need to work (dual incomes). Couples may delay having children or have fewer, which limits family size.

The recession after 2008 brought unemployment, mortgage arrears (missed home-loan repayments) and lower family incomes. Some families moved in with relatives, and adult children stayed at home or returned to it, giving multi-generation households.
Emigration and mobility for work, especially in recessions, mean parents or adult children live abroad, so the family is spread across countries. A parent may also work away from home.
Women's paid employment has increased, so many mothers work outside the home. This increases the demand for childcare and changes who earns and who cares in the family.

Changes in work, such as shift work, part-time work, flexible hours and hybrid working (part at home, part in the workplace), change how caring time is shared. Farming is no longer the main source of income for farm families.
Unemployment, especially long-term, reduces family income. This increases the financial burden and stress, and can bring conflict within the family.

Families on a low income, lone-parent families and the unemployed depend on State support. State supports such as welfare, Child Benefit and childcare schemes affect the choices families make, for example whether a parent stays at home or returns to work.
notes.tip: 'The recession happened' earns no marks. Say what it did to the family, such as adult children staying at home, giving extended households. Remember dual incomes are an effect of women's employment and high costs, and also a cause of demand for childcare.

notes.h: Technological changes affecting family structure (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Technology has changed how families are formed, how housework is done and how members keep in touch. It affects family size, family roles and how family life is lived day to day.
points: Contraception allows couples to decide whether and when to have children, which affects family size and timing.

Assisted human reproduction, such as fertility treatment, allows some couples who could not otherwise have children to do so. The Health (Assisted Human Reproduction) Act 2024 regulates it and was enacted in 2024, though only some of its sections are in force so far.

Household appliances such as washing machines, dishwashers, microwaves and smart appliances save time on housework. This frees parents for paid work, leisure and children, and makes shared household roles easier.

Communication technology such as mobile phones, email, video calls and social media keeps family members in contact across distance and time zones. It helps emigrant families and separated parents, but it can reduce face-to-face contact.
Social media and screens also bring pressures, including cyberbullying and pressure on children.

Remote working lets parents work from home, and online services such as banking, shopping, and school and health information save time on household administration. Parents can therefore combine work and care.
Computers and the internet support learning, while screens and games change how families spend time together. Home security systems and monitoring give families safety.
Medical technology and better healthcare lower child mortality and lengthen life, so families are smaller and there are more older family members.
notes.tip: Marking schemes list communication and social media, home working and online services, household appliances, and entertainment and security technology. Use the pattern change, effect on the family, example.

notes.h: Combined effects of social, economic and technological change (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The three kinds of change rarely act alone. Their effects overlap, and together they explain the shape of families today.
points: High housing costs plus recession: adult children remain in the family home or return to it, creating an extended household.
Emigration plus communication technology: the family is split across countries but can be in daily contact by video calls and messages.
Remote working plus childcare costs: a parent can combine paid work with caring for children at home.
Divorce plus communication technology: separated parents in different households keep shared parenting arrangements going through video calls and messages.
Overall, families are smaller, more varied (nuclear, lone-parent, blended, same-sex and cohabiting) and more mobile, with more flexible roles and more reliance on State and private services.
notes.tip: A high-scoring answer takes about four to six developed points with at least one from each of the social, economic and technological headings, each stating the change and its effect on the family. Questions may ask about one heading only, or the effect on one structure such as lone-parent or extended families, so link changes to structures.

keyTerms.definition: Two unmarried adults living together as a couple in a shared home.
Medical techniques, such as fertility treatment, that help couples to conceive a child.
A couple in which both partners pursue paid careers.
The movement of people from rural areas to towns and cities.
A family whose members live in different countries but remain connected.
Paid work carried out from home or another location away from the employer's premises.
Repayments on a home loan that have fallen due but have not been paid.
Tension that arises when the demands of two or more family or work roles clash.

factCards.term: Three social changes that increased the number of lone-parent and blended families
factCards.definition: Divorce and separation; remarriage; births outside marriage.

factCards.term: Three economic pressures on Irish families since 2008
factCards.definition: Unemployment and mortgage arrears; emigration; rising housing and childcare costs.

factCards.term: Three technologies that changed family life
factCards.definition: Household appliances; mobile phones and video calls; contraception and assisted reproduction.

factCards.term: Effect of the recession on living arrangements
factCards.definition: Adult children stay at home or return, creating extended households.

factCards.term: Effect of a parent working abroad on family structure
factCards.definition: The family is split between countries, with parents and children living apart.

factCards.term: Two ways social media can affect family communication
factCards.definition: Cyberbullying can be carried out at home; face-to-face conversation can be reduced.

questions.prompt: Name two social changes that have affected family structure and explain how each has done so.
questions.model: Two social changes, each with explanation. For example: divorce and separation, which have increased lone-parent and blended families as partners separate and form new unions; later marriage and smaller families, as couples have fewer children later in life. Other accepted examples: births outside marriage, cohabitation, or gender equality leading to dual-career couples.

questions.prompt: Assess how economic and technological changes have affected family life and family structures in Ireland, giving examples.
questions.model: Economic change: recession after 2008 brought unemployment, mortgage arrears and emigration, so families split or adult children remained at home, creating extended households. Rising housing and childcare costs make two incomes necessary, delaying or limiting family size. Women's paid work means many mothers work outside the home. Technological change: contraception and assisted human reproduction let couples choose the timing and size of their families. Household appliances reduced housework and freed parents for paid work. Mobile phones and video calls keep relatives in contact across borders, supporting transnational families. Remote working lets parents combine paid work with childcare at home. Social media brings new pressures, including cyberbullying. Assessment: economic pressures change the structure of families most directly, while technology mainly changes how family members manage their roles and stay in touch.
